claim: Temple-worship sermon; quotes Brigham Young that the endowment enables one to 'walk back to the presence of the Father … and gain your eternal exaltation,' but adds no axis-specific content.
quote: Your endowment is, to receive all those ordinances in the house of the Lord, which are necessary for you, after you have departed this life, to enable you to walk back to the presence of the Father … and gain your eternal exaltation.

claim: Adversity and Atonement sermon; the only exalt* token is inside a quoted D&C 121 promise, with no doctrinal claim on any axis.
quote: And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.

claim: McMullin opens by naming as an 'overarching truth of the Restoration' that God is an exalted man with a body of flesh and bones, and in the same sentence insists He is 'yesterday, today, and forever the same unchangeable God' — the King Follett premise asserted alongside strict immutability, the same exalted-man-plus-fixed-perfection pairing that made Milton R. Hunter Oct 1948 a false negative.
quote: One of the overarching truths of the Restoration is that God lives and dwells in His heavens, that He is an exalted man with “a body of flesh and bones,” and that He is yesterday, today, and forever the same unchangeable God, the fountain of all virtue and truth.

claim: Celestial marriage sermon quoting the family proclamation's 'heavenly parents' and D&C 131's three levels within the celestial glory, closing with a D&C 93 theosis line; eternal increase, new spirit children, and divine ancestry are all conspicuously absent.
quote: As Jesus ultimately received the fulness of the glory of the Father, so we may “come unto the Father … and in due time receive of his fulness.”

claim: Adversity sermon; no axis content beyond a quoted D&C 121 'God shall exalt thee on high.'
quote: And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.

claim: Covenant sermon that reaches exaltation and cites D&C 132:20 — the 'then shall they be gods' verse — but renders its content only as 'all the divine possibilities God can give,' a euphemism rather than a claim.
quote: If we are faithful to the covenants made there, we become inheritors not only of the celestial kingdom but of exaltation, the highest glory within the heavenly kingdom, and we obtain all the divine possibilities God can give (see D&C 132:20).

claim: Apologetic on the breadth of the plan of salvation versus sectarian hell; exaltation appears only as the destination of the faithful, with no axis-specific content.
quote: Their true destination was paradise followed by exaltation in the celestial kingdom.

claim: In an adversity sermon with no exaltation vocabulary, Eyring states that the purpose of mortal trial is to prepare us to be entrusted with 'an endless posterity' whom we will ourselves teach and lead through tests so they can qualify for eternal life — the forward chain (B3) asserted plainly by a member of the First Presidency, with our future role explicitly parallel to God's present one.
quote: We will become able to want what God wants, to think as He thinks, and thus be prepared for the trust of an endless posterity to teach and to lead through tests to be raised up to qualify to live forever in eternal life.

claim: Two accounts of families bearing bereavement; sealing and the covenant appear, but the only exalt* token is the quoted D&C 121 promise and there is no axis content.
quote: And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high; thou shalt triumph over all thy foes.

claim: Administrative address on Relief Society purpose and meeting policy; 'prepared for eternal life' is as far as it reaches, with no axis content.
quote: Ours is the priesthood purpose to prepare ourselves for the blessings of eternal life by making and keeping covenants.

claim: Callister enumerates four First Vision truths — separate beings, glorified bodies of flesh and bones, open heavens, apostasy — and argues from God's sameness 'yesterday, today, and forever'; corporeality and immutability are touched but 'God was once a man' is conspicuously not among the four restored truths.
quote: The second great truth Joseph Smith discovered was that the Father and the Son have glorified bodies of flesh and bones.

claim: Sermon on bearing burdens; perfection is named as the eventual end and D&C 121's 'God shall exalt [us] on high' is quoted, but nothing axis-specific follows.
quote: Burdens provide opportunities to practice virtues that contribute to eventual perfection.

claim: Covenant history from Adam to the modern gathering of the Gentiles; exaltation appears twice as the universal promise, without any claim about its content.
quote: The love of our Father in Heaven has been evident as the way has been opened for all living and dead of every nation, now and in the future, to receive exaltation in His presence, according to the exercise of their agency.

claim: Tyndale-framed sermon on scripture; God's power 'to save and exalt His children' and 'our divine potential' are the only axis-adjacent phrases, both generic.
quote: Through the scriptures, God does indeed “show forth his power” to save and exalt His children.

claim: Family history sermon that defines being exalted purely as dwelling with extended family in God's presence; sealing chains run backward to ancestors, never forward to offspring of the exalted.
quote: We are exalted when we can dwell together with our extended families in the presence of Almighty God.

claim: Fairy-tale-framed young women's address; closes with the temple-adjacent image of daughters of God as 'princesses, destined to become queens' and quotes the Young Women theme's 'blessings of exaltation,' but the royalty language stays metaphorical with no doctrinal claim attached.
quote: You are truly royal spirit daughters of Almighty God. You are princesses, destined to become queens.

claim: Names exaltation as the purpose of life and speaks of developing 'the attributes of godliness,' but the content of exaltation is left as receiving all of Heavenly Father's blessings.
quote: Our purpose in life is to gain eternal life and exaltation for ourselves and to help others do the same.

claim: Tribute to the ordinary faithful; 'plan for salvation and exaltation' is named once in passing with no doctrinal development.
quote: The personal value, the sacred splendor of every one of you is the very reason there is a plan for salvation and exaltation.

claim: Missionary-work sermon; 'salvation and exaltation' and 'divine destiny' appear only as incidental phrases.
quote: Your friends, in the comfort of your home and with your constant reassurance, can begin their journey toward salvation and exaltation.

claim: Sermon on faith and character formation; exaltation is mentioned once only to say material things do not lead there.
quote: Nor do they lead us to exaltation.

claim: Welfare and service sermon; 'exalts' appears once as a verb describing what charitable service does for the receiver, with no axis content.
quote: Helping one another is a sanctifying experience which exalts the receiver and humbles the giver.

claim: Welfare history sermon that ties caring for the poor to inheriting 'the full measure of eternal life' and learning 'the celestial principles of sacrifice and consecration'; exaltation is invoked as an outcome without content.
quote: As sons and daughters of God, we cannot inherit the full measure of eternal life without being fully invested in caring for each other while we are here on earth.

claim: Chastity sermon calling procreation 'a sacred and exalted power' for bringing pre-existing spirits into bodies, plus the sealing-room mirrors and the Young Women theme; all mortal procreation and premortal spirits, nothing about spirit offspring of the exalted.
quote: You understand that you possess a sacred power that involves the holy responsibility of bringing other spirits to earth to receive a body in which to house their eternal spirit.

claim: Priesthood-session talk on learning in quorums; premortal preparation of 'we spirit sons' and one incidental 'lead toward exaltation' are the only axis-adjacent phrases.
quote: You will find joy in the happiness of those you lead toward exaltation.

claim: Temple-building sermon; the blessings of the temple are described as returning to Heavenly Father in an eternal family relationship and being endowed with power, closing on 'eternal life and exaltation' without further content.
quote: They understand that the saving ordinances received in the temple that permit us to someday return to our Heavenly Father in an eternal family relationship and to be endowed with blessings and power from on high are worth every sacrifice and every effort.

claim: Elijah and family history sermon; 'the work of salvation and exaltation' is a refrain but exaltation's content is never specified beyond sealing the generations backward.
quote: We are the Lord’s agents in the work of salvation and exaltation that will prevent “the whole earth [from being] smitten with a curse” (D&C 110:15) when He returns again.

claim: Titanic-framed sermon on tragedy and unfulfilled potential; the three-act premortal/mortal/eternal framing and one 'salvation and exaltation' phrase are the extent of it.
quote: His Son, Jesus Christ, is our Savior and Redeemer, whose Atonement not only provides for salvation and exaltation but also will compensate for all the unfairness of life.

claim: Enumerating the Abrahamic covenant's promises, Nelson lists 'entitled to an eternal increase' alongside numerous posterity and the priesthood, then chains D&C 84 — receive the priesthood, receive Christ, receive the Father, 'receive all that He has' — and names celestial marriage 'the covenant of exaltation'; eternal increase is asserted as a covenant entitlement, though Nelson never says what increases, so this is B1 only and thinner than the Penrose 1911 calibration case.
quote: Abraham’s posterity would be numerous, entitled to an eternal increase, and also entitled to bear the priesthood.

claim: Sermon on human insignificance against cosmic scale that quotes 'Worlds without number have I created' and then promises 'exaltation—worlds without end—within our grasp'; the juxtaposition flirts with the plurality-of-worlds inheritance but 'worlds without end' is used in its KJV sense of endlessness, so no claim is actually made.
quote: We have the incomprehensible promise of exaltation—worlds without end—within our grasp.

claim: History of prophetic counsel to Relief Society, closing with a Lorenzo Snow quotation promising sisters a share 'in the exaltation and glory which the Lord will give'; generic.
quote: As you have shared in these labors, so you will most certainly share in the triumph of the work and in the exaltation and glory which the Lord will give to His faithful children.

claim: Christofferson lays down the modern rule that a single leader's statement, past or present, need not be doctrine, and reprints J. Reuben Clark's warning about 'adventurous expeditions of the brethren into these highly speculative principles and doctrines' whose announcers later Presidents judged not moved upon by the Holy Ghost — the canonical mechanism by which nineteenth-century teachings on divine ancestry and progression get bracketed; important caveat, he names no specific doctrine, so this is meta-level reframing rather than the softening of an identified teaching.
quote: It is commonly understood in the Church that a statement made by one leader on a single occasion often represents a personal, though well-considered, opinion, not meant to be official or binding for the whole Church.

claim: Reactivation sermon; 'exalting covenants' appears once as a phrase with no doctrinal content.
quote: After all, that is what priesthood service is all about—bringing all people to the exalting covenants; bringing peace, happiness, and self-worth.

claim: Sealing-power sermon quoting D&C 130's 'same sociality' and D&C 121's promise of 'an everlasting dominion' to faithful fathers; dominion language appears but only as quoted scripture, with no claim about what the exalted receive.
quote: The Holy Ghost shall be thy constant companion, and thy scepter an unchanging scepter of righteousness and truth; and thy dominion shall be an everlasting dominion, and without compulsory means it shall flow unto thee forever and ever.

claim: Priesthood-duty sermon; quotes Joseph Smith that priesthood 'existed with God from eternity … without beginning of days or end of years' and warns that losing priesthood power loses 'the essence of exaltation,' but neither line is developed.
quote: If we are not worthy, it is possible to lose the power of the priesthood; and if we lose it, we have lost the essence of exaltation.

claim: Gratitude sermon that opens with God as Father of our spirits with 'a glorified, perfected body of flesh and bone' and later states divine immutability in contrast to human changeability; immutability is asserted but only as a homiletic premise for repentance, never as a position on divine progression.
quote: God is the same yesterday, today, and forever, but we are not.

claim: Testimony-versus-conversion sermon built on Peter and the ten virgins; 'ordinances and covenants of salvation and exaltation' is a single incidental phrase.
quote: As we honor the ordinances and covenants of salvation and exaltation (see D&C 20:25), “press forward with a steadfastness in Christ” (2 Nephi 31:20), and endure in faith to the end (see D&C 14:7), we become new creatures in Christ.

claim: Relief Society address on caregiving; the only exalt* token is the quoted D&C 121 promise, used to frame enduring trials well.
quote: And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.

claim: Priesthood-path sermon framing the oath and covenant as a climb toward receiving 'all that the Father hath' and an 'exalted destination'; the D&C 84 phrase is quoted without unpacking.
quote: In that covenant is embedded a glorious journey that begins with receiving both the lesser and higher priesthoods, progresses through magnifying our callings, and climbs ever upward to God’s grandest vistas, until we receive “all that [the] Father hath.”

claim: Family history and vicarious ordinance sermon; quotes Howard W. Hunter on 'the priesthood temple ordinance work necessary for our own exaltation' but never says what exaltation consists of.
quote: We must accomplish the priesthood temple ordinance work necessary for our own exaltation; then we must do the necessary work for those who did not have the opportunity to accept the gospel in life.

claim: Priesthood-session talk framed by two flying experiences; the priesthood is called 'the eternal power and authority of God' through which He 'redeems and exalts His children,' with no content on the exalted state.
quote: Through this power, He redeems and exalts His children, bringing “to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.”

claim: Chastity sermon grounded in the family proclamation's 'heavenly parents' and mortal procreation as a delegated portion of God's creative power; its sharpest line defines damnation as arrested progression toward becoming like Heavenly Father, which implies continued development for the exalted but stays on the theosis axis and says nothing about spirit offspring or divine ancestry.
quote: One of the potent scriptural meanings of the word damned is illustrated in his inability to continue developing and becoming like our Heavenly Father.

claim: Sermon on personal versus universal peace; the sole exalt* token is the quoted D&C 121 promise, and the celestial kingdom appears only as the destination of covenant families.
quote: And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.

claim: Young women's address on standing firm; calls procreation 'an exalted power' (quoting Oaks) and future motherhood 'an exalted role,' and describes the body as housing 'the eternal spirits of others who will come to the earth as part of your eternal family' — mortal procreation of premortal spirits, not postmortal spirit offspring.
quote: Because it has the capacity to house not only your eternal spirit but also the eternal spirits of others who will come to the earth as part of your eternal family.

claim: Unpacking the Young Women theme, Dalton predicates exaltation of God Himself — 'We are daughters of an exalted being!' — the outgoing Young Women general president asserting in general conference that Heavenly Father occupies the exalted state, the same construction that made Milton R. Hunter's 1948 'exalted man' a false negative; caveat, the line is a single undeveloped exclamation and 'exalted' could be read adjectivally as simply 'most high.'
quote: It is not only an affirmation of our identity—who we are—but also an acknowledgment of whose we are. We are daughters of an exalted being!

claim: Sermon on doing things the Lord's way; 'we are not spiritual orphans' develops divine parentage only as an analogy about having parents to learn from, and exaltation is mentioned once in passing.
quote: Jesus is our Savior and Redeemer, who through the Atonement made it certain we will overcome death and live again and possible for us to be exalted and have eternal life.

claim: Obedience sermon that quotes D&C 93:28 three times and calls it 'What a glorious promise!' — the obedient will be glorified in truth and know all things; a human-omniscience promise, but delivered as scriptural quotation with no doctrinal development and nothing said about God's own knowledge or progression.
quote: He that keepeth [God’s] commandments receiveth truth and light, until he is glorified in truth and knoweth all things.

claim: Nelson mentions that the Restoration made 'knowledge and essential ordinances for salvation and exaltation' available and that exaltation means dwelling with family in God's presence, but says nothing about how or whether that entails godhood, divine parenthood, or a chain of gods.
quote: Ultimately, that exaltation allows each of us to dwell with our families in the presence of God and Jesus Christ forever!

claim: Maynes uses 'salvation and exaltation' and 'God shall exalt thee on high' purely as motivational framing for enduring trials; no content on divine progression, ancestry, or spirit offspring.
quote: The Savior’s atoning sacrifice makes possible our future salvation and exaltation through the principle of repentance.

claim: A single passing reference to bringing the less-active 'to eventual exaltation'; the talk is entirely about home teaching.
quote: Ours is the responsibility to teach, to inspire, to motivate, and where we visit those who are not active, to bring to activity and to eventual exaltation the sons and daughters of God.

claim: Oaks makes the structural assertion that Latter-day Saint theology *begins* with heavenly parents (plural) and that the fulness of eternal exaltation is attainable only within a family/marriage relationship — a specific, quotable modern apostolic statement of divine parentage plus relational exaltation, though it stops short of new spirit children or a backward chain.
quote: Our theology begins with heavenly parents, and our highest aspiration is to attain the fulness of eternal exaltation.

claim: Generic covenant/exaltation framing — 'receive all that the Father hath' and 'worthy to receive exaltation and eternal life' — with no specification of what exaltation consists of.
quote: The trials and tribulation that we experience may be the very things that guide us to come unto Him and cling to our covenants so that we might return to His presence and receive all that the Father hath.

claim: Temple/family-history talk; asserts generically that 'the celestial organization of heaven is based on families' and that vicarious work lets us 'be exalted as well as saved,' with no content on divine ancestry, divine progression, or spirit offspring.
quote: This is because the celestial organization of heaven is based on families.

claim: In a bulleted list of restored truths Corbridge calls God 'a personal, exalted being' and says humans 'may become like Him' — bare theosis plus an adjective that gestures at King Follett without asserting God's past mortality, His Father, or His continued progression.
quote: God is a personal, exalted being, an Eternal Father. He is our Father.

claim: Priesthood keys/authority and women; the only axis-adjacent lines are a generic 'qualifying for exaltation' aside and J. Reuben Clark's line about women's power to be 'a creator of bodies,' which concerns mortal birth, not divine viviparous mechanism.
quote: Latter-day Saints surely recognize that qualifying for exaltation is not a matter of asserting rights but a matter of fulfilling responsibilities.

claim: Packer, as an ordained apostle, gives an explicit promise that eternal increase — eternal parenthood — will not be withheld from the faithful who go without marriage or children in mortality, framing parenthood itself as an eternal (not merely mortal) blessing.
quote: We do not always know how or when blessings will present themselves, but the promise of eternal increase will not be denied any faithful individual who makes and keeps sacred covenants.

claim: Covenant-path talk for women; mentions only that temple ordinances are 'necessary for our exaltation in the celestial kingdom' without saying what exaltation consists of.
quote: They are those ordinances necessary for our exaltation in the celestial kingdom.

claim: Passing references to 'separation from our heavenly parents' and 'the exaltation He planned for us'; the talk is a Christ-as-exemplar sermon with no axis content.
quote: I am certain we left our Father with an overwhelming desire to return to Him, that we might gain the exaltation He planned for us and which we ourselves so much wanted.

claim: Allan F. Packer uses 'qualifying for exaltation' as an extended passport metaphor for meeting gospel requirements; exaltation's content is never specified.
quote: Qualifying for exaltation is like entering another country. We must each obtain our spiritual passport.

claim: Uchtdorf, in the First Presidency, teaches that we are 'children of heavenly parents' and anchors it with an explanatory footnote reaffirming Joseph F. Smith's literal spirit-birth doctrine — men and women are *literally* God's offspring, begotten and born of heavenly parents and reared to maturity before mortality; the body of the talk also promises D&C 132:19's 'thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers, dominions.' Conflation note: the load-bearing viviparous language sits in a footnote, not the spoken text.
quote: President Joseph F. Smith taught that “man, as a spirit, was begotten and born of heavenly parents, and reared to maturity in the eternal mansions of the Father, prior to coming upon the earth in a temporal [physical] body”

claim: Marriage-and-complementarity talk; generic 'covenant sons and daughters of our loving heavenly parents' plus a Benson quote on the 'salvation and exaltation of your families.' The claim that Satan 'has forfeited that sacred privilege of ever becoming a husband or father' gestures at eternal parenthood but is not developed.
quote: He has forfeited that sacred privilege of ever becoming a husband or father.

claim: Christofferson lays out explicit tripartite staging — pre-existent intelligences were 'given form, or spirit bodies, by God,' thereby becoming His spirit children — an organization account of spirit origin rather than a viviparous birth account; he grounds the plan in Joseph Smith's line that God instituted laws so lesser intelligences 'could have a privilege to advance like himself,' and asks whether we can 'be trusted both in time and eternity with godly powers, including power to create life.'
quote: Prophets have revealed that we first existed as intelligences and that we were given form, or spirit bodies, by God, thus becoming His spirit children—sons and daughters of heavenly parents.

claim: Family-proclamation defense; the only axis-adjacent line is that the fulness of priesthood blessings requires a sealed husband and wife. No content on divine ancestry, progression, or spirit offspring.
quote: For anyone to attain the fulness of priesthood blessings, there must be a husband and a wife sealed in the house of the Lord, working together in righteousness and remaining faithful to their covenants.

claim: Boyd K. Packer's last conference address makes the procreative power itself the mechanism of deification: righteous exercise of it can bring 'a fulness of joy, even godhood'; he cites D&C 132:19's 'continuation of the seeds forever and ever,' promises 'eternal increase' to the worthy, and grounds the whole in Abraham 4:27's plural 'the Gods' — the clearest generative-exaltation statement in this chunk.
quote: Through the righteous exercise of this power, we may come close to our Father in Heaven and experience a fulness of joy, even godhood.

claim: Sitati links the Genesis charges (be fruitful, multiply, subdue) to becoming as God is, but the multiplying in view is mortal childbearing that gives bodies to God's pre-existing spirit children; he never asserts eternal increase, new spirit offspring, or any backward chain. Near-miss on B — the procreation-to-godlikeness link is explicit but stops at mortality.
quote: Heavenly Father has charged and blessed us to be fruitful, to multiply, and to subdue the earth that we might become like Him.

claim: Easter grace sermon; bare theosis only — grace grows us into 'exalted beings' and 'all that the Father hath shall be given unto us,' with no specification of godhood's content.
quote: If salvation means only erasing our mistakes and sins, then salvation—as wonderful as it is—does not fulfill the Father’s aspirations for us. His aim is much higher: He wants His sons and daughters to become like Him.

claim: Discipleship talk that defines salvation as the highest degree of glory and refers to God's 'expectation that we become as He is' — bare theosis with no further specification.
quote: Allow me to share four key principles that will help us fulfill our desire to be responsible to our Father in Heaven as well as respond to His expectation that we become as He is.

claim: Standard premortal-spirit-children framing (Adam and Eve and their posterity create mortal bodies for God's spirit children) plus generic 'exaltation is the goal of this mortal journey'; nothing on divine ancestry, progression, or postmortal spirit offspring.
quote: It was their charge—and, subsequently, the charge of their posterity—to create mortal bodies for God’s spirit children so they could experience mortality.

claim: Ecclesiology talk; the only axis-adjacent line is a generic progression statement grounded in D&C 93:13 ('from grace to grace, until we receive a fulness'), with no specification of what that fulness is.
quote: It is important to recognize that God’s ultimate purpose is our progress. His desire is that we continue “from grace to grace, until [we receive] a fulness” of all He can give.

claim: Shark-barrier analogy for commandments; a single generic reference to being 'exalted in the next' life.
quote: The Lord’s commandments are given out of love and caring; they are intended for our joy in this life just as much as they are intended for our joy and exaltation in the next.

claim: Call for women's influence in the Church; exaltation appears once as the destination of the covenant path, with no doctrinal specification and no Heavenly Mother content.
quote: We need women who are devoted to shepherding God’s children along the covenant path toward exaltation; women who know how to receive personal revelation, who understand the power and peace of the temple endowment

claim: Reeves rebroadcasts Boyd K. Packer's 'even godhood' claim verbatim in general conference six months after he gave it, endorsing procreative power as the means of attaining godhood, and adds that mortal bodies are made for God's 'beloved spirit children' and that the faithful will receive 'all that [our] Father hath.' Conflation note: the doctrinal content is Packer's (2015 April, 'The Plan of Happiness'), quoted approvingly rather than independently formulated.
quote: Through the righteous exercise of this [creative] power, we may come close to our Father in Heaven and experience a fulness of joy, even godhood.

claim: Contrasts telestial salvation with celestial exaltation and cites 'all that the Father hath shall be given unto us' — the standard formula, with no specification of godhood, posterity, or divine ancestry.
quote: As members of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, we aspire to something unimaginably greater. It is exaltation in the celestial kingdom.

claim: Comfort-in-affliction talk; quotes Brigham Young on sanctification crowning one 'with immortality and eternal lives' and Lorenzo Snow on the faithful receiving every blessing, but neither is developed and the technical sense of 'eternal lives' is never unpacked.
quote: It is, for my will to be swallowed up in the will of God, that will lead me into all good, and crown me ultimately with immortality and eternal lives

claim: Eyring, in the First Presidency, closes by naming 'the promise of an endless posterity' as the supernal blessing priesthood holders should qualify for, and opens by describing the premortal family with 'our exalted and eternal Heavenly Father' whose kind of life (eternal life) we are to live — explicit endless posterity rather than generic exaltation.
quote: Among those “many things” is the promise of an endless posterity.

claim: Hallstrom builds an entire talk on literal divine parentage as the Church's 'most fundamental doctrine,' assembling the canonical proof-text set (Moses 1:13; Psalm 82:6; Acts 17:29; D&C 76:24's 'begotten sons and daughters unto God'; the family proclamation's 'beloved spirit son or daughter of heavenly parents') and making heavenly parentage the precondition of exaltation. Conflation note: asserts *our* divine parentage only — nothing about God the Father's own parentage or progression.
quote: A correct understanding of our heavenly heritage is essential to exaltation.

speaker: Neill F. Marriott
claim: Neill F. Marriott quotes the teaching that faithful suffering makes people more like their Father and Mother in Heaven.

Priesthood-power sermon; notes that the priesthood is the same power by which God 'created this and numberless worlds' and 'exalts His obedient children,' and quotes George Albert Smith on qualifying for 'positions that our Father expects us to fill hereafter' — suggestive but unspecified.
quote: Think of this: the priesthood conferred upon us is the very same power and authority through which God created this and numberless worlds, governs the heavens and the earth, and exalts His obedient children.

claim: Hymn-history and humility talk; a single generic reference to exaltation as the destination reached through the 'valley of humility.'
quote: All of us look forward to exaltation, but before this can occur, we must persevere through what has been referred to as the “valley of humility.”

claim: Systematic treatment of faith-repentance-baptism-Holy Ghost-enduring; exaltation and becoming 'perfected like the Savior' appear as generic endpoints, with D&C 93's 'grace for grace … until we receive a fulness' cited but not unpacked.
quote: As we continue in this process and obtain all the saving ordinances and covenants of the gospel, we receive “grace for grace” until we receive a fulness.

claim: Talk on Church callings; quotes Marion G. Romney that service 'is the very fiber of which an exalted life in the celestial kingdom is made' and notes that through service 'we become more like God' — bare theosis.
quote: Service is not something we endure on this earth so we can earn the right to live in the celestial kingdom. Service is the very fiber of which an exalted life in the celestial kingdom is made.

claim: Grace-and-worthiness talk; exaltation and the celestial kingdom appear only as the destination the repentant will reach, with no doctrinal content about what exaltation is.
quote: The great news is that if we have sincerely repented, our former sins will not keep us from being exalted.

claim: Pastoral talk on those who cannot yet 'sing'; a single passing phrase calls the plan 'His plan for our exaltation' with no doctrinal content.
quote: In this great oratorio that is His plan for our exaltation, may we humbly follow His baton and keep working on the songs we cannot sing

claim: A whole apostolic address on the nature of God the Father that conspicuously brackets His origin: Oaks says we 'know comparatively little about Him,' endorses Bruce R. McConkie's maximal formulation that in the ultimate and final sense there is only one true and living God — the Father, Supreme Being, Creator and Ruler of the universe — and cites the 1909 'Origin of Man' and 1916 'Father and the Son' statements while saying nothing of King Follett, God's own progression, or Heavenly Mother. A datapoint for the modern reticence/reframing posture rather than for any positive regress claim.
quote: In the ultimate and final sense of the word, there is only one true and living God. He is the Father, the Almighty Elohim, the Supreme Being, the Creator and Ruler of the universe.

claim: Compassion-for-sinners sermon; the exaltation content is the standard formula — choose to become like Him, qualify for the kind of life He enjoys, become heirs to all He has. Conflation note: the supporting footnote cites D&C 132:19–20, 24, 55 (the 'then shall they be gods' and 'continuation of the seeds' verses) but the body never unpacks them.
quote: No, our Heavenly Father desires that His children knowingly and willingly choose to become like Him and qualify for the kind of life He enjoys. In doing so, His children fulfill their divine destiny and become heirs to all that He has.

claim: Talk against fear-based motivation; one generic clause describes God's work and glory as being to 'mentor us, exalt us, and lead us to His fulness.'
quote: His very purpose—His work and His glory—is to mentor us, exalt us, and lead us to His fulness.

claim: Sermon on holiness and the sacrament; theosis appears only as 'internalize the qualities and character of Christ' and Romney's 'exalted life' line. Near-miss worth noting: Christofferson glosses Moses 6:57's 'Man of Holiness is his name' as a recognition of the Father's divinity and holiness, using the anthropomorphic title without drawing any inference about God's own manhood or past.
quote: Enoch’s statement makes it clear that these references are actually a recognition of His divinity and holiness—He is the Son of Man of Holiness, God the Father.

claim: Women's-session talk on President Kimball's 1979 prophecy; one generic closing line that God's work and glory is 'the exaltation and eternal life of women and men.'
quote: His work and glory is the exaltation and eternal life of women and men.

claim: Oaks defines exaltation as intrinsically familial rather than individual — 'exaltation in families,' quoting Nelson that salvation is individual but exaltation is a family matter — reaffirms the proclamation's claim that gender is an essential characteristic of premortal, mortal, and eternal identity, gives the insider account of the proclamation's 1993–95 drafting, and closes by citing D&C 131:1–4 (the increase passage) as the warrant. Conflation note: relational/generative exaltation is asserted structurally but new spirit offspring are never named.
quote: While there are various kingdoms and glories, our Heavenly Father’s ultimate desire for His children is what President Monson called “eternal life in the kingdom of God,” which is exaltation in families.

claim: Conversion narrative built on a childhood question — will you still be my mother in heaven? — answered by the missionaries with eternal parent-child relations; the 'nature of God' section affirms only a tangible embodied God and that trials let us 'become like Him.' Eternal parenthood is illustrated, never doctrinally specified.
quote: They taught us that families truly can be together after this life as father, mother, and sons and daughters.

claim: Oath-and-covenant of the Melchizedek Priesthood presented in standard form — the faithful holder 'along with his wife' becomes joint-heir with Christ to the Father's kingdom. Conflation note: a footnote quotes Bruce R. McConkie that God swears 'that we will have a like exaltation' as Christ, but the body never develops what that exaltation consists of.
quote: He will become heir to the blessings of Abraham and, along with his wife, joint-heir with Jesus Christ to Heavenly Father’s kingdom.

claim: Talk on the Church as people rather than institution; one generic clause names Christ's Atonement and covenants as 'the only pathway to salvation and exaltation.'
quote: This Church belongs to Him, and His sanctifying Atonement and covenants are the only pathway to salvation and exaltation.

claim: Forgiveness talk built on the speaker's family losing a brother to a drunk driver; exaltation appears once, as the generic outcome of ordinances and covenants.
quote: And by receiving necessary ordinances, keeping covenants, and obeying commandments, we can gain eternal life and exaltation.

claim: Repentance-and-second-chances talk; theosis appears rhetorically ('our nature is no longer human but divine') and the closing testimony invokes capitalized 'Heavenly Parents' and 'Their presence' — a Heavenly Mother usage datapoint but not a claim about Her.
quote: If to err is human nature, how many failures will it take us until our nature is no longer human but divine?

claim: Newly called apostle's first address, on prophetic authority; exaltation appears once in the closing testimony with no content.
quote: I testify that He is the Savior and Redeemer of the world and that through Him we can be saved and exalted in the presence of our dear God.

claim: Easter sermon on the Resurrection; the exaltation content is two words — 'purified and exalted' — with no doctrinal specification.
quote: We can become purified and exalted.

claim: Catalogs the saving ordinances (baptism, confirmation, Melchizedek ordination, endowment, sealing) as those 'essential to our exaltation,' quoting True to the Faith; exaltation itself is never defined.
quote: Through His Atonement, Jesus Christ redeemed us from the consequences of the Fall of Adam and made possible our repentance and eventual exaltation.

claim: The strongest hit in this chunk after Packer. Ashton states that in the premortal world 'we were born as spirits to Heavenly Parents' (footnoting both the family proclamation and the 'Mother in Heaven' Gospel Topics essay), enumerates the three explicit conditions for becoming like the Father — glorified immortal bodies, marriage sealed by priesthood power (citing D&C 132:19–20), and acquiring 'all knowledge, power, and divine attributes' — and speaks of 'what Heavenly Father has become,' language that presupposes divine becoming even as the same talk lists 'He does not change' among His attributes. He also concedes in a footnote that God has not revealed the process of becoming like Him and that he does not know all the reasons why.
quote: Given the distance between what we are as mortals and what Heavenly Father has become, it is not surprising that some feel that becoming like the Father is unattainable.

claim: Announces the rationale for the 2018 two-hour block and home-centered curriculum; the Church's mission is stated generically as assisting God 'to bring to pass the salvation and exaltation of His children.'
quote: all of these interrelated actions are part of a unified effort to better align the focus, resources, and work of the Savior’s restored Church with its fundamental mission: to assist God in His work to bring to pass the salvation and exaltation of His children

claim: Eyring, in the First Presidency, states the coupled-exaltation doctrine in its flattest, most quotable modern form: husband and wife are 'equal in their divine destiny to be exalted together,' and exaltation is categorically unavailable to an individual alone. Conflation note: asserts that exaltation requires the couple, not that exalted couples beget spirit children; compare Oscarson 2015 April, which makes the same point in weaker, priesthood-blessings language.
quote: They are equal in their divine destiny to be exalted together. In fact, men and women cannot be exalted alone.

claim: Closing conference remarks and temple announcements; exaltation appears once as a generic reason for temple attendance.
quote: We know that our time in the temple is crucial to our salvation and exaltation and to that of our families.

claim: The 'correct name of the Church' address; the only axis-adjacent language is a generic clause about the Atonement's power 'ultimately to exalt us,' plus the standard note that Christ under the Father's direction created 'this and other worlds.'
quote: If we as a people and as individuals are to have access to the power of the Atonement of Jesus Christ—to cleanse and heal us, to strengthen and magnify us, and ultimately to exalt us—we must clearly acknowledge Him as the source of that power.

claim: Oaks opens the talk by identifying children as 'our eternal increase' — deploying the technical D&C 131/132 term for exalted posterity and applying it directly to mortal childbearing, then arguing from declining birthrates that these trends work against the plan of salvation. Conflation note: the reframing runs the other direction from the 19th-century usage — 'eternal increase' is attached to children born in mortality rather than to spirit offspring begotten after exaltation.
quote: Children are our most precious gift from God—our eternal increase.

claim: Pieper says taking Christ's name upon us leads to becoming like Him and to exaltation in the celestial kingdom, but only in bare theosis terms.
quote: As we take upon us the Savior’s name, we truly lay hold upon every good thing and become like Him.

claim: Callister frames the Atonement as enabling us to become like God and to inherit thrones and kingdoms, but the claim never goes beyond generic theosis.
quote: I bear my witness that the Savior’s Atonement is not only infinite in scope but also individual in reach—that it can not only return us to God’s presence but also enable us to become like Him—the crowning goal of Christ’s Atonement.

claim: Nelson urges covenant-keeping so families may be exalted forever and returns to 'Heavenly Parents' only as boilerplate, with no claim about God's own origin, progression, or spirit offspring.
quote: My dear brothers and sisters, Jesus Christ invites us to take the covenant path back home to our Heavenly Parents and be with those we love.

claim: A talk on learning and teaching the gospel in the home; no content on any axis.
quote: Our purpose as we seek to learn and to teach the gospel of Jesus Christ must be to increase faith in God and in His divine plan of happiness and in Jesus Christ and His atoning sacrifice and to achieve lasting conversion.

claim: Cordon announces the revised Young Women theme naming 'heavenly parents' and calls the young women literal spirit daughters, but this is the Proclamation's standard premortal-parentage formula with no claim about God's origin, progression, or new spirit offspring of exalted couples.
quote: You are literally the spirit daughters of Heavenly Parents, and nothing can separate you from Their love and the love of your Savior.

claim: Oaks explicitly narrows what counts as official doctrine about the next life, ruling that leaders' individual statements and personal visions about post-mortal conditions are not binding doctrine and should not be taught as such.
quote: But let us not teach or use as official doctrine what does not meet the standards of official doctrine.

claim: Oaks ties exaltation to the male-female procreative power continuing eternally, glossing D&C 132:19's "continuation of the seeds forever and ever" as part of eternal life and describing exaltation as gaining "the exalted life and divine potential of our Heavenly Parents."
quote: Eternal life includes the creative powers inherent in the combination of male and female[^12]—what modern revelation describes as the “continuation of the seeds forever and ever.”

claim: Generic references to returning to "their heavenly parents" and fulfilling "divine potential" with no specific claim on any axis.
quote: They were focused on helping their children also understand and embrace those principles that would make them happy in this life, as well as prepared to return to their heavenly parents after having increased their abilities and proved their obedience to God.

claim: A missionary-work and Resurrection talk; the only contact with the axes is the boilerplate phrase "ordinances of salvation and exaltation," with no claim about deification, divine parentage, or divine progression.
quote: The priesthood ordinances of salvation and exaltation were prepared for every individual, including those who no longer dwell in mortality.

claim: A talk on Christ's Atonement as refuge in trials; no content on any axis beyond a scriptural 'God shall exalt thee on high' quotation.
quote: This single refuge provided by our Heavenly Father is our Lord Jesus Christ and His Atonement.

claim: Gong mentions the hope of exaltation and "our divine potential" to become more like the Savior, but makes no specific claim on any axis.
quote: Hallelujah expresses our praise to the Lord for the hope of salvation and exaltation.

claim: A talk explaining the principles behind the Children and Youth initiative; no content on any axis.
quote: I promise, as we focus on these principles—relationships, revelation, agency, repentance, and sacrifice—the gospel of Jesus Christ will sink deeper in all our hearts.

claim: Jones quotes President Nelson telling children that human progression continues after death and speaks of 'divine potential' and the work of exaltation, but makes no claim about God's own progression, origin, or spirit offspring.
quote: That's good, because we're always progressing. Even in the next life we're making progress.

claim: Standard plan-of-salvation summary: humans are to "be exalted and become like Him" and premortal spirits "desired to achieve the eternal life enjoyed by our heavenly parents," but no assertion of divine ancestry, God's own progression, or new spirit offspring.
quote: As spirits, we desired to achieve the eternal life enjoyed by our heavenly parents.

claim: Only a generic reference to being saved and exalted as a gift from Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ, with no claim about divine ancestry, God's progression, or generative exaltation.
quote: We have received life in this world; we will receive physical life in the hereafter, and eternal salvation and exaltation—if we choose it—all because of Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ.

claim: Salt Lake Temple history and a spiritual-foundation analogy; "exalted" appears only as an adjective for the temple building, and no axis content is present.
quote: As I contemplate the next four years of the life of this beautiful, noble, exalted, and awe-inspiring Salt Lake Temple, I envision it more as a time of *renewal* rather than a time of closure!

claim: A talk on speaking more openly of Jesus Christ; the only brush with the axes is one incidental word 'exalt' inside a quotation from President Nelson about the Church's name.
quote: If we … are to have access to the power of the Atonement of Jesus Christ—to cleanse and heal us, to strengthen and magnify us, and ultimately to exalt us—we must clearly acknowledge Him as the source of that power.

claim: One generic theosis clause ("strive to become like Him") plus a footnoted Lorenzo Snow assurance that the never-married faithful lose no "exaltation and glory"; no specific claim on any axis.
quote: When people love God with all their hearts and righteously strive to become like Him, there is less strife and contention in society.

claim: Youth-program talk with stock "work of salvation and exaltation" and "become more like Jesus" language; no specific claim on any axis.
quote: All Children and Youth activities and all Children and Youth teachings are about helping young people become more like Jesus by joining with Him in His work of salvation and exaltation.

claim: Oaks closes with generic "exaltation with our loving heavenly parents" boilerplate and nothing more specific.
quote: By understanding and conforming our lives to that doctrine, including the divine gift of repentance, we can be of good cheer as we keep ourselves on the path toward our eternal destiny—reunion and exaltation with our loving heavenly parents.

claim: Renlund speaks generically of qualifying to be saved and exalted and of assimilating God's attributes, with no claim about God's origin, God's own progression, or spirit offspring.
quote: We assimilate the attributes of Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ into our character, and we love one another.

claim: Generic spirit-children-of-heavenly-parents boilerplate (quoting the family proclamation) plus an assurance that faithful single members will have the opportunity for exaltation, with no claim about divine ancestry, God's progression, or new spirit offspring.
quote: Because we are the spirit children of God, everyone has a divine origin, nature, and potential.

claim: Ministering and outreach talk; no exaltation, deification, divine-parentage, or divine-progression content beyond the stock phrase "children of God" used to mean all people are siblings.
quote: They are all children of God, your brothers and sisters.

claim: Generic covenant-path framing in which exaltation is the unspecified end of the path; no claim about divine ancestry, God's own progression, or spirit offspring.
quote: In the course of the covenant path (which, by the way, extends beyond mortality), we receive all the ordinances and covenants pertaining to salvation and exaltation.

claim: Exaltation named only as an undefined blessing obtained through Christ, with no content on any axis.
quote: I testify of Him who died, was buried, and rose again the third day and ascended into heaven so that you and I receive the blessings of immortality and exaltation.

claim: Quotes the "thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers" clause of D&C 132:19 and speaks of "the beings of glory and grandeur we are designed to become," but stops short of the continuation-of-seeds clause and makes no claim about divine ancestry, God's progression, or new spirit children.
quote: That we will live forever, receive a fulness of joy,[^3] and have the potential to “inherit thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers.”

claim: Bednar uses the institutional phrase "work of salvation and exaltation" and generic becoming-like-God language without any specific axis claim.
quote: This family expressed sincere gratitude for the difficult mortal experiences that allow us to grow and become more like our Heavenly Father and our Redeemer, Jesus Christ.

claim: A talk on personal peace amid contention; the only near-axis language is the D&C 121 phrase 'God shall exalt thee on high' and a gloss about a celestial destiny, with no deification or divine-nature claim.
quote: It is clear that opposition can refine us for an eternal, celestial destiny.

claim: A humanitarian-aid report; 'work of salvation and exaltation' appears only as an administrative program label, with no axis content.
quote: The Church of Jesus Christ is under divine mandate to care for the poor.

claim: A talk on enduring suffering; contains no claim on any axis beyond quoting D&C 121:8 ('God shall exalt thee on high') in its consolation sense.
quote: “And then, if thou endure it well, God shall exalt thee on high.”

claim: Uses the stock phrase 'ordinances of salvation and exaltation' with no elaboration; no claim on divine ancestry, God's progression, or spirit offspring.
quote: Come unto Jesus Christ and choose to exercise your faith in Him; repent and make and keep the covenants found in the ordinances of salvation and exaltation.

claim: Stevenson uses "God's work of salvation and exaltation" as a program label and speaks of uniting families for eternity, with no specific claim on any axis.
quote: As we come unto Christ and help others do the same, we participate in God’s work of salvation and exaltation, which focuses on divinely appointed responsibilities.

claim: A talk on scripture study and conversion; 'plan of salvation and exaltation' and 'become like Him' appear only as passing phrases with no axis claim.
quote: As we study the scriptures, we will better understand God's plan of salvation and exaltation, and we will trust in the promises that He has made to us in the scriptures, as well as in the promises and blessings of modern prophets.

claim: A talk on the Church as its members; 'ordinances of salvation and exaltation' and 'become like Jesus Christ' are passing phrases with no axis claim.
quote: We are striving to become like Jesus Christ.

claim: Strongly affirms God's omniscience and omnipotence and the categorical gap between God and mortals, but frames it as a caution against judging God and never addresses whether God progresses; human destiny is described only as being heirs, not gods.
quote: Jehovah forcefully reminds Job of His omnipotence and omniscience, and Job in deepest humility admits he possesses nothing even close to the knowledge, power, and righteousness of God and cannot stand in judgment of the Almighty:

claim: Craven invokes "divine heritage," the handbook "work of salvation and exaltation," and becoming more like Christ, all generically.
quote: Our divine heritage gives us courage and confidence to do and be all that our loving Heavenly Father knows we can be.

claim: Kacher affirms generically that human progression is eternal and that exaltation is at stake, without any claim about God's origin, God's own progression, or spirit offspring.
quote: Our progression is an eternal one.

claim: Martinez's self-reliance talk mentions the "covenants and ordinances of salvation and exaltation" and becoming eternal families in passing, with no axis-specific claim.
quote: It will strengthen our faith in Jesus Christ and joyfully bind us to Him through the covenants and ordinances of salvation and exaltation.

claim: Nelson names exaltation as the destination of the covenant path but makes no specific claim about its content or about God's own nature.
quote: The covenant path is the *only* path that leads to exaltation and eternal life.

claim: Lays out three degrees within the celestial kingdom and says exaltation means becoming like the Father and the Son and requires eternal marriage, but stops at bare theosis: no divine ancestry, no divine progression, no spirit offspring, no Heavenly Mother.
quote: The highest of these is exaltation in the celestial kingdom, wherein we may become like our Father and His Son, Jesus Christ.

claim: Ojediran uses covenant-path and 'ordinances of exaltation' language and quotes Ballard that the precise time and manner of exaltation's blessings are unrevealed, but asserts nothing specific on any axis.
quote: Even though not all things have been revealed concerning "the precise time and manner in which the blessings of exaltation [will be] bestowed," we are nonetheless assured of them

speaker: Dale G. Renlund
claim: Dale G. Renlund affirms Heavenly Mother as revealed while fencing the subject with very-little-revealed language and prohibiting prayer to her.
A talk on Christ healing broken relationships and broken selves; no axis content at all (the word 'exalt' appears only in the ordinary sense of praising a person).
quote: I testify that there is nothing in your life that is broken that is beyond the curative, redeeming, and enabling power of Jesus Christ.

claim: Belonging/unity talk whose only axis contact is the stock phrase "ordinances" and "covenants of salvation and exaltation"; no specific claim on any axis.
quote: The Church is the custodian of the covenants of salvation and exaltation that God offers us through the ordinances of the holy priesthood.

claim: Cook's talk on testimony, bridling passions, and repentance speaks of returning to and living with God but contains no theosis, divine-ancestry, divine-progression, or heavenly-parents content.
quote: We cannot obtain the celestial kingdom and live with God the Father on borrowed light; we need our own testimony of Jesus Christ and His gospel.

claim: An explanation of why Latter-day Saints do not use the cross as an icon; 'exalting' appears once as an adjective for Christ's embrace, with no doctrinal content on any axis.
quote: It is one of the most powerful paradoxes of the Crucifixion that the arms of the Savior were stretched wide open and then nailed there, unwittingly but accurately portraying that every man, woman, and child in the entire human family is not only welcome but invited into His redeeming, exalting embrace.

claim: Bare theosis framed as grace-dependent transformation — we cannot exalt ourselves and can be changed to become as God is — with no claim about divine ancestry, God's progression, or eternal parenthood.
quote: Our Heavenly Father and our Savior, Jesus Christ, have the power to save us and transform us. They can help us become as They are.

claim: Pino names exaltation once as an eternal topic contrasted with mere taste preferences, without defining it or making any axis claim.
quote: However, exaltation is something much more transcendent than a sense of taste; it is a topic related to eternity.

claim: Defines exaltation as Christ's receiving "all that the Father has" and closes with the D&C 121:46 everlasting-dominion promise, but makes no claim about divine ancestry, the Father's own progression, or spirit offspring.
quote: The crown that Christ received by giving and doing all in His ability to set the pattern of loving the Father and loving us was to receive all power, even all that the Father has, which is exaltation.

claim: Bassett quotes Christofferson that God binds Himself to exalt us in exchange for covenant keeping, which is bare theosis language.
quote: In these divine agreements, God binds Himself to sustain, sanctify, and exalt us in return for our commitment to serve Him and keep His commandments.

claim: Corbitt gives the standard plan-of-salvation outline (God is the Father of our spirits; bodies in the image of His glorified body; eternal life with our families as He has with His) without asserting divine ancestry, God's progression, or new spirit children.
quote: Because He loves her and all His children, He made a plan for us to receive a body in the image of His glorified body,[^4] be part of a family,[^5] and return to His loving presence to enjoy eternal life with our families[^6] like He does with His.[^7]

claim: Closes with a bare theosis formula — to "be exalted and become like Him" — with no supporting claim on any axis.
quote: I testify that He did rise again on the third day and, having fulfilled the loving and infinite Atonement, stands with open arms, offering to us the opportunity to rise again, be saved, *and* be exalted and become like Him.

claim: Meurs describes the resurrected Christ as exalted and possessing all eternal power, but makes no claim about the Father's origin, progression, or spirit offspring.
quote: He was exalted and had all of His eternal power and capacity.

claim: Rasband's Palm Sunday talk speaks of living with Heavenly Father for eternity and mentions exaltation only generically in footnotes; the discourse carries no axis content.
quote: By divine design, His atoning sacrifice concluded His mortal ministry, making it possible for us to live with our Heavenly Father for eternity.

claim: Covenant-path talk that says covenants are grounded in "eternal, unchanging law" and lead to exaltation, and footnotes D&C 132:19-20 without quoting its gods/seeds language; no specific claim on any axis.
quote: Based on eternal, unchanging law, He specified the nonnegotiable conditions whereby we are transformed, saved, and exalted.

claim: Christofferson ties exaltation to sealed family relationships and to having eternal ancestry and posterity, but never asserts new spirit children, a mechanism, or anything about God's own lineage or progression.
quote: Without the sealings that create eternal families and link generations here and hereafter, we would be left in eternity with neither roots nor branches—that is, neither ancestry nor posterity.

claim: Parenting-focused talk; only generic theosis language, and only in a footnote quoting Renlund that God's goal is for children to 'ultimately become like Him.'
quote: Our Heavenly Father’s goal in parenting is not to have His children do what is right; it is to have His children choose to do what is right and ultimately become like Him.

claim: Devotional on 'spiritual face blindness' and seeing God as a loving Father; no claim touching divine ancestry, divine progression, or generative exaltation.
quote: We try to see through our covenants, as if through a window, to the face of the Father’s mercy behind.

claim: Covenant-path devotional; uses the standard 'heavenly parents' formula and generic becoming-language ('enable us to become as He is') without any specific claim about divine parentage or progression.
quote: I walk this path as a “beloved daughter of heavenly parents,” divinely known and deeply trusted.

claim: Nelson identifies procreative power as a specific attribute of godhood that God permits mortals to exercise — a quotable assertion that creating life is a divine, not merely mortal, prerogative.
quote: The power to create life is the one privilege of godhood that Heavenly Father allows His mortal children to exercise.

claim: Systematic treatment of the three degrees of glory and exaltation requirements; deification appears only as a quotation of D&C 76:58 ('they are gods') — bare theosis, no divine-ancestry or progression claim.
quote: This is the dwelling of those “who have received of his fulness, and of his glory,” wherefore, “they are gods, even the sons [and daughters] of God” and “dwell in the presence of God and his Christ forever and ever.”

claim: Asserts premortal divine sonship as identity ('always been a son or daughter of God') but makes no claim about God's own parentage, progression, or new spirit offspring.
quote: There is one important identity we all share now and forever. … That is that you are and have always been a son or daughter of God.

claim: Carpenter enumerates the blessings of exaltation as including 'a continuation of the seeds forever and ever' and quotes D&C 131 that the unsealed 'cannot have an increase' — eternal increase named as the specific content of exaltation.
quote: They include dwelling in God’s presence for eternity together as husband and wife, inheriting “thrones, kingdoms, principalities, and powers, … and a continuation of the seeds forever and ever,” receiving all that God the Father has.

claim: Sermon on the intent of the Father's plan as homecoming and mercy; no claim about divine ancestry, divine progression, or eternal increase.
quote: He wants to make it possible for every last one of His Father’s children to receive the end goal of the plan—eternal life with Them.

claim: Historical/doctrinal survey of covenants; exaltation is named as the goal of temple covenants but with no content beyond 'eternal life' and dwelling with God.
quote: The ordinances and associated covenants of the temple are requirements for exaltation in the celestial kingdom, which is eternal life, “the greatest of all the gifts of God.”

claim: Talk on affliction and joy; the only axis-adjacent line is a quoted Orson F. Whitney passage, with 'heavenly parents' substituted in brackets, about becoming more like them — bare theosis.
quote: It is through sorrow and suffering, toil and tribulation, that we gain the education that we come here to acquire and which will make us more like our [heavenly parents].

claim: Alliaud affirms from the general conference pulpit that God the Father 'is an exalted man' and draws the explicit symmetry that talking about God's nature is talking about our own, grounding literal (not metaphorical) divine sonship and human deification.
quote: We believe that God the Father “is an exalted man” with a glorified “body of flesh and bones as tangible as man’s; [and] the Son also.” Thus, every time we talk about the nature of God, in some way, somehow, we are also talking about our own nature.

claim: Traces a woman's progression from daughter in the kingdom to 'elect lady' to 'queen'; female deification language only, with no assertion of eternal increase, Heavenly Mother, or divine ancestry.
quote: This tiny daughter has the potential to become an elect lady in His kingdom and eventually a queen.

claim: Testimony that mortality is designed to work through trial; no claim on any axis beyond quoting Moses 1:39.
quote: God’s work and glory is to bring to pass the immortality and eternal life of man.

claim: Christological sermon; the only axis-adjacent language is 'divine DNA' applied to Jesus's victories and a generic reference to the Church as the vehicle of exaltation.
quote: Jesus was routinely placed in difficult, often devious situations in which He was always triumphant—victories for which we have no explanation except divine DNA.

claim: Talk on trusting God's definitions of right and wrong and submitting one's will; no axis content.
quote: God has established these boundaries Himself, based on eternal truths for our benefit and blessing.

claim: Dynamite analogy for gospel-plus-Church; exaltation appears only as 'co-inheritor' language in a footnote — bare theosis.
quote: His goal has been to refine you into pure gold, to save and exalt you as a co-inheritor with Him in the kingdom of our Heavenly Father.

claim: Forward-looking talk on the 2024–2034 decade; touches premortal existence only through a quoted George Q. Cannon line about spirits reserved for this dispensation.
quote: God has reserved spirits for this dispensation who have the courage and determination to face the world and all the powers of the evil one [and to] … build up the Zion of our God fearless of all consequences.

claim: Opens with the standard catechetical chain — God is our spirit parent, we are His spirit children, therefore we can become like Him — but states it only in the generic curricular form with no further specification.
quote: God is our Father in Heaven. We are His spirit children, and we are created after His image. Therefore, each of us, as a child of God, has a divine potential to become like Him.

claim: Compensating-blessings talk; quotes Lorenzo Snow that the faithful who lacked opportunity will still have 'all the blessings, exaltation and glory' — exaltation asserted as universally attainable but with no content specifying what exaltation consists of.
quote: There is no Latter-day Saint who dies after having lived a faithful life who will lose anything because of having failed to do certain things when opportunities were not furnished him or her. … They will have all the blessings, exaltation and glory that any man or woman will have who had this opportunity.

claim: Primary-focused believe/belong/become talk; theosis appears generically in the body and in a footnote quoting Joseph Fielding Smith on the faithful increasing 'in knowledge, wisdom, and power' — human, not divine, progression.
quote: They shall increase in knowledge, wisdom, and power, going from grace to grace, until the fulness of the perfect day shall burst upon them.

claim: Talk on Primary music; asserts literal divine childhood and divine potential in testimony-list form without further specification.
quote: I know that we are literal children of God, created in His image, endowed with divine potential, and invited to return to live with Him if we choose to follow Jesus Christ.

claim: Talk on convert growth and welcoming new members; exaltation is framed procedurally as the set of covenants to receive, with no doctrinal content about its nature.
quote: Focus on the covenants necessary for exaltation. The gospel makes exaltation possible, which requires the making and keeping of sacred covenants with God.

claim: Talk on gospel simplicity and his grandmother's faithfulness in isolation; 'God's work of salvation and exaltation' appears only as a program name.
quote: We focus on “the things that matter most” in God’s work of salvation and exaltation instead of getting caught up in managing our ministering.

claim: Sermon on being proved and strengthened through trial; no axis content beyond a quotation of D&C 121:8 ('God shall exalt thee on high').
quote: He is making you strong enough to carry the weight of eternal life.

claim: Administrative talk on ministering by 'counting and accounting' for members by name; 'salvation and exaltation' appears only as the program name.
quote: And so it should be for each of us, as instruments in His hands in His amazing work of salvation and exaltation.

claim: Frames the whole plan as familial from premortal council to eternal destiny and repeats 'exaltation is a family affair,' but stops short of asserting eternal increase, heavenly parenthood, or divine ancestry.
quote: We can truly say that the gospel plan was first taught to us in the council of an eternal family, it is implemented through our mortal families, and its intended destiny is to exalt the children of God in eternal families.

claim: Five parallels between a named professorship and taking on Christ's name; closes with generic joint-heir/exalted-inheritor language.
quote: You will become an exalted inheritor in the kingdom of our Father in Heaven, a joint-heir with His Firstborn, our beloved Savior and Redeemer.

claim: Andersen names 'thrones, powers, and dominions in the eternal world' as the promised reward of temple sealing, and the published footnote quotes the General Handbook that the highest blessing of the everlasting covenant is 'exaltation with eternal posterity' — eternal increase stated as the content of exaltation in a 2026 conference talk.
quote: We solemnly vow to keep the covenants, and the Lord promises us, as we are faithful, unspeakable blessings in mortality and beyond, including thrones, powers, and dominions in the eternal world.

claim: Talk on loving 'all' and 'each'; the only axis-adjacent line is a generic reference to seeing others' capacity to become exalted beings.
quote: We begin to see them as the Lord sees them—mortal souls with the capacity to become exalted beings through the Savior’s restoring power and grace.

claim: Easter litany of the names of Christ; exaltation appears only in a quoted Renlund phrase about what covenants do.
quote: His covenants bind us to Him—so He can “transform, save, and exalt” all who choose Him.

claim: Part-member-family talk; quotes Oaks that the plan's destiny is 'to exalt the children of God in eternal families' and calls the sealing the crowning ordinance, but adds no claim about increase or divine ancestry.
quote: Because of Jesus Christ, all can receive the gift of eternal life—which includes living in God’s presence eternally as families.

claim: Anti-Edmunds-law and temperance discourse that closes with a pro-natalist appeal grounding celestial marriage in an 'eternal law of increase' and God's glory in perpetuating life, but the increase in view is mortal begetting of tabernacles for waiting spirits, not postmortal divine increase.
quote: God has His glory in the perpetuation of life. With wonder and admiration, we behold life everywhere. … All nature responds to the eternal law of increase.

claim: Kimball states the backward chain explicitly: we return to our Father and God, who is connected to a Father still farther back, and that Father to another, indefinitely — a regress of Gods asserted from the conference pulpit.
quote: We must be grafted into the true vine, and continue to partake of its fatness, and then we shall go back to our Father and God, who is connected with one who is still farther back; and this Father is connected with one still further back, and so on; and just so far as we respect our superiors and try to save our children, so shall we receive blessings from this time forth and forever, and shall become as numerous as the sands upon the seashore.

claim: Brief third-person report of Grant's remarks on the antipolygamy raid, charity toward persecutors, and the Word of Wisdom; no axis content.
quote: If we at any time undertook to pull down the religious idols of the age, we also offered to show in place thereof, the true and living God, and to tell mankind how to approach and worship Him acceptably.

claim: Relief Society talk on strengthening families; asserts a premortal 'heavenly family' as the prototype of earthly families and quotes Benson promising mothers 'all that the Father hath,' but both in the standard generic register.
quote: In the premortal existence, our heavenly family was a prototype for us to follow in guiding our families here on earth.

claim: Talk on simplifying life around four key relationships; asserts spirit childhood and 'divine potential' in the standard generic form.
quote: First, our relationship with God is most sacred and vital. We are His spirit children. He is our Father.

claim: Survey of priesthood keys across three historical scenes; asserts premortal spirit childhood and quotes Brigham Young that priesthood is the law by which the worlds continue, but makes no claim about God's own origin or progression — the closing hymn's refrain 'Our fathers' God is still the same' is devotional, not doctrinal argument.
quote: Scene one pertains to keys of the priesthood in ancient days, even before creation of the earth. We then existed as spirit children of God.

claim: Easter retelling of 3 Nephi; quotes D&C 76:24 on plural worlds whose inhabitants are 'begotten sons and daughters unto God' without comment or development.
quote: That by him, and through him, and of him, the worlds are and were created, and the inhabitants thereof are begotten sons and daughters unto God.

claim: Talk on enduring trials well; references premortal spirit children and the Abraham 3 proving council in passing.
quote: They are about us, those of the spirit children of our Heavenly Father who would come into mortality.

claim: Scott states the three-stage anthropology in passing but explicitly — intelligences tabernacled with spirits, who then receive a body — a compressed but quotable apostolic affirmation of tripartite staging in a 2010 conference talk otherwise about the Atonement.
quote: What eternal purpose would have come from the Creation of the earth, where intelligences tabernacled with spirits would receive a body, if death were the end of existence and none would be resurrected?

claim: Anti-pornography address that makes procreative power the center of the plan and denies it to Satan, and quotes Abraham 4's plural 'the Gods' without comment; specific about mortal procreation but silent on eternal increase or divine ancestry.
quote: The adversary is jealous toward all who have power to beget life. Satan cannot beget life; he is impotent.

claim: Systematic treatment of death, paradise, resurrection, judgment, and eternal life; defines eternal life as the kind of life God lives and closes with the plural 'eternal lives,' but never unpacks either into increase or divine ancestry.
quote: After judgment comes the possibility of eternal life—the kind of life that our Heavenly Father lives.

claim: Repentance and forgiveness talk; the only axis-touching phrase is the boilerplate that all humans are God's spirit children except the Only Begotten.
quote: Knowing that all of His spirit children save His Only Begotten, Jesus Christ, would unintentionally or intentionally violate His laws, our Eternal Father provided a means to correct the consequences of such acts.

claim: Session-by-session minutes index for the October 1859 conference, not a discourse; it preserves Brigham Young's 'spirit begets spirit—likeness, likeness' fragment and points to his Oct. 9 'Intelligence, Etc.' discourse, but the claims belong to those underlying sermons.
quote: President Brigham Young spoke on "Blessings of Association—Original Purity of the Human Spirit—Trials and Temptations, &c," urging Saints to "diffuse light and knowledge" while keeping "bad feelings" private: "spirit begets spirit—likeness, likeness."

claim: Talk on strengthening and rescuing youth; frames mortality as a journey home for God's spirit children without further axis content.
quote: Brothers and sisters, our Heavenly Father wants and needs our help to bring His spirit children home to Him again.

claim: Missionary-couple recruitment talk built on the Good Samaritan; asserts universal divine fatherhood as the ground of human brotherhood but nothing further.
quote: A more perfect parable could not have been conceived to teach the eternal truth that God is the Father of us all and therefore we are brothers one to another.

claim: Priesthood-session survey of Restoration doctrine; assembles premortal foreordination, uncreated intelligence (D&C 93:29), plural inhabited worlds whose inhabitants are 'begotten sons and daughters unto God,' and endorses singing 'O My Father' — but each as a citation rather than a new claim.
quote: Not only was Jesus “in the beginning with God,” but “man was also in the beginning with God. Intelligence, or the light of truth, was not created or made, neither indeed can be.” … We can thus sing “O My Father” with real intent and assurances of real belonging.

claim: Kapp reads into the October 1986 conference record a young woman's letter naming Heavenly Mother alongside Heavenly Father, and speaks in her own voice of 'our heavenly home and parents' — a dateable pulpit assertion of Heavenly Mother five years before Hinckley's 1991 caution. Caveat: the naming occurs inside quoted correspondence, endorsed rather than authored by Kapp.
quote: I just wish of all things I could go up and give Heavenly Father and Heavenly Mother a big hug and tell them that I made it back.

claim: Featherstone asserts in his own voice that women's traits descend 'from a divine mother' / 'heavenly mother,' and states that every young woman may bear a child 'either in this life or in the eternal worlds' — an explicit viviparous claim about postmortal childbearing from the general conference pulpit in 1987.
quote: Worlds without end, men will never be able to bear children. Every young woman may be a procreator with God and carry a little one under her breast either in this life or in the eternal worlds.

claim: Komatsu quotes Orson F. Whitney's consolation passage in its original wording — 'more like our Father and Mother in heaven' — into the 1987 conference record; the same Whitney passage is quoted in 2024 by Brian K. Taylor with the phrase bracketed out and replaced by '[heavenly parents]', making this pair a documented reframing over time.
quote: it is through sorrow and suffering, toil and tribulation, that we gain the education that we come here to acquire and which will make us more like our Father and Mother in heaven
